input:
Current use

Electricity use at the brewery amounts to 1689 MWh per year. The site load is divided between the brewhouse, the cellar and cold store, the packaging lines and the utility plant, and the metered total represents the sum of those uses over the course of the year. Refrigeration accounts for the largest share of the total, and the refrigeration section below deals with that share in greater detail. Steam is raised on site for the brewhouse and for cleaning purposes, and its figures rest on a considerably shorter measurement period than the electricity figures; the steam section sets out the basis, and the recommendation draws out the consequence for the saving case. It should be emphasised that no part of the assessment rests on nameplate ratings: the electricity figure is metered consumption, and the projected saving is stated against that metered figure.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest single use of electricity on the site. The load is continuous in character: fermentation vessels are held at controlled temperatures, finished beer is held cold, and glycol is circulated to the vessel jackets and to the cold store, so the compressors run through the day and the night rather than simply following the brewing programme. Because the load runs continuously, a saving in the refrigeration system is repeated in every operating hour of the year, and refrigeration is where a heat-recovery retrofit finds both its heat source and much of its recovered duty. Heat rejected at the condensers is available at a temperature that is well suited to preheating water for the brewhouse and for cleaning, duties that would otherwise be met from steam. The assessment treats the refrigeration plant as the point of recovery and the hot-water demand of the brewhouse as the point of use, and the projected saving is an electricity saving at the refrigeration plant together with the steam saving that follows from the displaced water heating; the steam part of the benefit is the part that is qualified in the recommendation. Compressor condition, suction and discharge pressures and glycol temperatures were all reviewed as part of the assessment, and no defect was found that would change the saving case: the projected saving is a recovery opportunity on plant that is working as intended, rather than a repair saving on plant that is not.

Steam

Steam serves the brewhouse vessels, the cleaning-in-place station and space heating, and it represents the second energy stream considered in the assessment. The steam figures are drawn from one winter month. Winter is the season of highest steam demand on this site: space heating is at its peak, incoming water is at its coldest, and the brewhouse works against the largest temperature lift of the year. A saving rate that is measured or estimated on a winter month therefore reads high when set against the year as a whole, and steam savings stated from that month would overstate the annual figure if they were carried across the year without correction. The assessment does not correct the steam figures to an annual basis, because no second measured month exists against which to correct them; the figures are presented as winter-month figures and are used in the recommendation only with that qualification firmly attached. The electricity figures are not affected by the same qualification, since they rest on a full year of metering.

Recommendation

A heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant is projected to save 11% of electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 186 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $274k. At $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out at $22295, and the derived simple payback is 12.3 years. The payback is long when set against the life usually asked of refrigeration plant work, and it is stated on the electricity saving alone. It is important to note that the steam figures in this assessment are taken from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal: any steam saving added to the case would be stated on a winter basis and would tend to flatter the payback, so no steam saving has been counted in the figures above. The recommendation is that a decision on the retrofit be taken on the electricity case as stated, with the payback of 12.3 years clearly in view, and that the steam benefit be treated as unquantified until steam metering has covered a summer month as well as a winter one.

The condensers reject heat that the compressors have lifted from those cold duties, together with the compressor work itself, which is why the heat available at the condensers is larger than the cooling duty it came from. The assessment does not correct the steam figures to an annual basis, because no second measured month exists to correct them against; the figures are presented as winter-month figures and are used in the recommendation only with that qualification attached. Boiler operation, condensate return and distribution losses all sit inside the steam figures as measured, and the assessment does not separate them, because the metering on which the figures rest does not separate them either. Electricity figures are not affected by the same qualification, since they rest on the full year of metering.

Recommendation

A heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant is projected to save 11% of electricity use, a derived saving of 186 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $274k. Metering the steam over a full year, or at least over contrasting seasons, is the step that would put the steam part of the case on the same footing as the electricity part of it.
